nameStory: The "common" sea star earned its name by being the most abundant and familiar starfish along the northeastern Atlantic coast, including New England's shores. It's also called the "sugar starfish" because of its slightly granular, sugar-like texture when you gently touch its surface. The scientific name "rubens" means "reddish," referring to its typical orange to brownish coloration.
description: The common sea star is exactly what most people picture when they think "starfish" — a five-armed marine animal with a classic star shape. These sea stars typically span 4-12 inches across, though exceptional individuals can reach over 20 inches from arm tip to arm tip. They're usually orange, brown, or sometimes violet in color, with pale specimens found in deeper waters. Their bodies feel firm and slightly bumpy to the touch, with a texture reminiscent of coarse sandpaper.

idTips.label: Five-armed star shape
idTips.description: Always has exactly five thick, tapering arms radiating from a central disc, creating the classic starfish silhouette that's unmistakable

idTips.label: Orange to brown coloration
idTips.description: Typically bright orange, rusty brown, or brownish-red, though deeper water specimens appear much paler or whitish

idTips.label: Granular texture
idTips.description: Surface feels like coarse sandpaper or sugar crystals when gently touched, created by tiny calcium carbonate bumps called ossicles

idTips.label: Tube feet underneath
idTips.description: Flip it over to see hundreds of small, soft tube feet arranged in grooves along each arm — they feel squishy and may still be moving

idTips.label: Firm, thick arms
idTips.description: Arms are substantial and chunky, not thin or delicate, and feel solid when gently squeezed

habitat: Look for common sea stars in rocky tide pools, on gravelly shores, and attached to pier pilings and jetties along New England's coast. They prefer areas with hard surfaces where they can hunt for mussels, clams, and other shellfish. You'll often find them in the low tide zone and shallow subtidal areas, especially around mussel beds and oyster reefs.

seasonality.spring: Most active as waters warm up, often found in shallow tide pools during low tides. This is prime time for tide pooling and spotting them.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're easiest to observe feeding and moving around. Commonly seen during summer tide pooling expeditions.
seasonality.fall: Still active but may move to slightly deeper waters as temperatures drop. Good time to find them on dock pilings and breakwaters.
seasonality.winter: Less active and often in deeper water, but can still be found in protected tide pools during warmer winter days.

funFact: A common sea star can push its entire stomach out through its mouth to digest prey externally — it literally wraps its stomach around a clam, digests the meat outside its body, then pulls its stomach back in!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Forbes's sea star, but the common sea star typically has a more granular, bumpy texture and tends to be more orange, while Forbes's is often smoother and more purple or reddish. When in doubt, the common sea star's "sugar crystal" texture is your best clue.
contextualKnowledge: Many people call them "starfish," but they're not fish at all — they're echinoderms, more closely related to sea urchins and sand dollars. Marine biologists prefer "sea star" to avoid this confusion, though both names are widely accepted.
compareHints: The common sea star differs from its close relative Forbes's sea star primarily in texture and color. Common sea stars have that distinctive granular, sugar-like surface texture and lean toward orange-brown colors, while Forbes's sea stars are typically smoother to the touch and more purple or deep red in color. Both have five arms and similar size, making texture your best distinguishing feature.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Forbes's Sea Star differs from its close relative, the Common Sea Star, primarily in color preference and habitat.
